clinical_record:
A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. She was in good general condition, weighed 5 kg, had an oxygen saturation of 80%, and showed no signs of respiratory distress. Her medications included furosemide and spironolactone. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. Approximately 12 hours after the procedure, the patient developed clonic movements of the left upper limb and persistent sucking motions. A noncontrast head CT obtained after this first seizure showed a slight diffuse increase in cortical density predominantly in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and, to a lesser extent, in the left parietal and occipital lobes; there was no mass effect, hemorrhage, or other intracranial abnormality.

A 52-year-old man presented with sudden, pressure-like, substernal chest pain that started at rest and radiated to the left jaw, associated with nausea, dyspnea, and diaphoresis. Symptoms began approximately 6 hours before arrival. Two hours after intervention, the patient reported a new onset of fever and worsening chest pain that was retrosternal and sharp in quality, but not affected by positional changes or exertion.

Initial examination: Patient was tachycardic, with no murmurs. No crackles were present on lung auscultation. Jugular venous pressure was normal. Follow-up examination: Temperature of 38.3°C, auscultation revealed a new pericardial friction rub located over the left sternal border.

- Laboratory Tests:
Initial troponin levels were 14 µg/L

- Imaging Studies:
1. Initial ECG showed ST-segment elevations in leads II, aVF, and V3-V5
2. Coronary angiography findings: acute thrombotic total occlusion of the mid-segment of the left anterior descending artery with TIMI 0 flow. Ventriculography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 55% to 60%
3. Second ECG: complete resolution of ST-segment elevation in V2-V3 with persistence of ST-segment elevation in II, III, aVF, and V4-V6 without reciprocal changes
4. Third ECG (24 hours later): diffuse ST-segment elevation on II, III, aVF, and V3-V5 accompanied by PR-segment depression in I and II and PR-segment elevation in aVR without reciprocal changes
5. Transthoracic echocardiogram: no evidence of pericardial effusion, no wall motion abnormalities, ejection fraction of 55% to 60%

A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. 

On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. 

Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.

An 18-month-old girl was brought for evaluation of a swelling in her left medial thigh. Over the past six months, the mass had enlarged gradually and was painless, with no history of trauma or infection. On examination, there was a firm, nonpulsatile mass measuring approximately 10 cm, fixed to underlying tissues but mobile relative to the overlying skin. There were no signs of inflammation, neurovascular impairment, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory tests were unremarkable. A CT scan of the thigh showed a well-defined, lobulated, hypodense mass in the left anteromedial compartment of the proximal thigh, extending toward the inguinal area. The lesion exhibited internal septations and a density similar to subcutaneous fat, displacing the common and superficial femoral vessels anterolaterally without signs of invasion; it abutted the proximal femoral bone but did not erode it.

An MRI confirmed a fatty-appearing, well-circumscribed mass with internal septations and no encasement of neurovascular structures.

A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned. She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation. She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy.

On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.” A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area. There were no signs of steroid-induced atrophy, such as skin thinning or increased vascular prominence.

An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

A 49-year-old woman was referred for surgical management of a presumed large nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma. She reported a 2-year history of chronic bitemporal headache, unexplained easy fatigability, and very slowly progressive diminution of vision. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, visual acuity was decreased bilaterally (worse on the left) with bitemporal homonymous hemianopia. Endocrinological evaluation revealed central hypothyroidism, and levothyroxine replacement was initiated. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a slightly hyperdense large sellar/suprasellar mass extending into both cavernous sinuses with right parasellar extension and bony remodeling of the sella turcica and upper clivus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 36 × 41 × 50 mm sellar/suprasellar/parasellar mass with heterogeneous low T1 signal, intermediate high T2 signal, small central areas of diffusion restriction on DWI, and mild patchy postcontrast enhancement. The lesion encased the cavernous and clinoid segments of the right internal carotid artery and partially encased the left cavernous segment. The optic nerves and chiasm were elevated and inseparable from the mass, and the pituitary gland and stalk were not visualized.

An 80-year-old woman was referred for management of a chronic superficial sacral wound present for approximately 2 years. She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. Her history was notable for inverse psoriasis affecting the natal cleft, prior coccygectomy 20 years earlier, multiple cutaneous nonmelanoma skin cancers, ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, hypertension, dyslipidemia, mild asthma, and splenectomy. Medications included aspirin, rosuvastatin, valsartan, and topical corticosteroids as needed.

On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well. The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 6 × 13 × 28 mm area of nonspecific, irregular superficial enhancement in the natal cleft without invasion of underlying structures, no visible sinus tract, and no regional nodal or bony metastases. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease.

A 62-year-old man presented with a two-week history of an asymptomatic swelling in the right lower half of the face and reduced mouth opening. He reported two prior similar episodes over eight years: the first, five years ago, was treated as a buccal-space infection with incision and drainage; the second, two years ago, resolved spontaneously. He had no pain or fever and was a known diabetic on regular medication. 

On examination, there was gross right facial asymmetry. Extraorally, a 6 × 6 cm ovoid subcutaneous swelling extended from the level of the right lateral canthus to 1 cm below the corner of the mouth and from the corner of the mouth posteriorly to the mandibular ramus. The borders were ill-defined, the consistency ranged from soft to firm, and the overlying skin was normal. There was no lymphadenopathy, paresthesia, or facial palsy. Intraorally, the right buccal mucosa was elevated and glistening, with no vestibular obliteration; mouth opening was restricted by the mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the face showed a well-defined soft-tissue mass with cystic areas in the right buccal space. Intracystic loculations with dense cystic content were noted, and there was erosion of the posterior buccal cortex without perforation of the maxilla; the maxillary antrum was compressed.

A clinical diagnosis of a nonspecific chronic abscess with buccal-space involvement was made. Under general anesthesia, an intraoral approach was used to excise the lesion in toto with a margin of fibrous tissue. The lesion shelled out easily, with no involvement of buccinator muscle or bone. The excised specimen measured 4.8 × 4.5 cm, was creamish-brown, firm, irregular, and had a leathery pouch-like appearance, entirely within the soft tissue of the buccal space.
